conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that based on current clinical evidence, ivermectin does not lower the risk of death in COVID-19 patients and is not an effective treatment for reducing mortality. Thus, it clearly rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
Based on current clinical evidence, ivermectin does not lower the risk of death or improve critical outcomes in COVID-19 patients. 

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that although ivermectin may alleviate some symptoms, it did not significantly improve critical clinical outcomes such as mortality, ICU admissions, or ventilator use (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40110299/). Similarly, the large-scale PRINCIPLE trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* found that early treatment with ivermectin did not lower the incidence of hospital admission or prolonged emergency department observation among outpatients (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869). 

The IVERCOR-COVID-19 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial also found that ivermectin had no significant effect on preventing hospitalizations in patients with COVID-19 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8250562/). 

Reflecting this lack of proven efficacy, the FDA has not approved ivermectin for treating or preventing COVID-19, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends against using it for outpatients with COVID-19 outside of a clinical trial context (https://www.healio.com/news/primary-care/20201208/this-was-a-gift-to-us-ivermectin-effective-for-covid19-prophylaxis-treatment). Therefore, the evidence supports that ivermectin is not an effective treatment for reducing mortality in COVID-19.
